lines.text: Hi, I'm Sindy! Today, we break a cluster on purpose.
A node dies halfway through a job. Does your job script cope? Does your workflow tool notice? Better find out on a cluster nobody needs.
Say you run a Slurm site, or you build a tool that submits jobs to Slurm, like a workflow manager or a web portal.
You need to know what happens when nodes join, hang or die, and when the controller fails.
We'll rehearse all four on throwaway clusters. All you need is sind and Docker.
First, a quick refresher on node states. An idle node has no jobs, and an allocated node is busy running them.
slurmctld pings every slurmd. When a node stops answering, its state gets a star, like idle star.
If it stays silent for the slurmd timeout, slurmctld marks it down and schedules nothing there.
Once slurmd registers again, the return to service setting that sind uses brings it back.
First cluster: plain sind create cluster gives you a controller and one worker.
Drill one, nodes join: sind create worker adds three more. It writes them into the Slurm configuration, reconfigures slurmctld, and starts slurmd.
Drill two, a node hangs. sind power freeze pauses every process on worker zero. Its container still shows as running, but nothing inside answers.
slurmctld shows it as idle star after a failed ping, and as down about five minutes later, with the default slurmd timeout.
Unfreeze it, and once slurmd registers again, the node is back in service.
Drill three, nodes die. sind power cut kills all four workers at once, like a rack that loses power.
This is the moment to watch your tools. Does the workflow manager notice? Does it resubmit?
Once they're down, sind power on starts them again, and they return to service the same way.
And when a node leaves for good, sind delete worker takes it out of the Slurm configuration before it deletes the container.
Waiting five minutes per drill adds up. So for drills, set a shorter slurmd timeout, in the main part of the slurm section.
Set it to thirty, and a lost worker turns down in about thirty to forty seconds instead.
But careful: on an overloaded CI runner, a short timeout also marks a slow but healthy node down, which kills its jobs.
Drill four, the controller fails. This config builds a second cluster, dev, where a backup controller stands next to the primary, plus two workers.
Create it with the config flag, and sind returns once both controllers answer.
sind get cluster lists the pair, and the star after primary marks the controller in charge.
Now freeze the primary. Once it has been silent for the slurmctld timeout, twenty seconds here, the backup takes over.
Both controllers share the saved state, so the backup carries on with the queue.
A frozen primary wakes up without knowing it was replaced. So unfreeze it, and restart its slurmctld to hand control back.
Finally, scontrol ping confirms that both controllers are up again.
To sum up: sind power breaks nodes on purpose, and Slurm notices them through missed pings.
Lower the slurmd timeout for quick drills, and add a backup controller to rehearse failover.
Next up: Slurm in your pipeline. See you there!
